Title: morning shrine
Author: Veronica P. '27
Article Content:
this morning i was awake at 6am. on the other end of one of those things i do where i allow myself to fall asleep, once my brain has settled to mush and past it’s point of productivity, and i tell myself that when i wake up early the next morning, i will be clean, shiny, and focused, and do all the work i want to do. in this grey-blue light i am not quite clean, shiny, or focused, but i am renewed and on my way to being those things. the sweat of a sleep well slept is sticking onto my skin, and the weight of my blanket is insisting that i don’t have to be at my meeting until 11:30. why not stay a while?
when i wake up i face the side of my dresser. i’ve taped a sign my friend made when i picked her up from the airport my sophomore year: “HAPPY BDAY VERO <3.” last spring i added, atop the dresser, a box from my roommate that reads, “RONNIE’S 21st!” the idea of these being the first words i read each morning reminds me of a taylor swift lyric. i don’t love it, but i have enough nostalgic sentimentality towards t.s. to know it: “I’m so depressed, I act like it’s my birthdayyyyy every day!” it doesn’t quite apply, at least currently. maybe it can be called a preventative measure.
last spring i also added, to this morning shrine, an award i got from doing well in one of my classes. it is the single most tangible piece of academic validation that i have gotten at this institution, so i cherish it with A+ fridge-magnet levels of pride. for some reason, when i look at it this morning, i think of a conversation i had at 3am this past summer, on a rooftop on beacon st.
in the midst of catch-up, i mentioned that i had just decided to try for grad school, post-MIT. a good friend, the second friend i ever made at this school, overhears and interjects with an exaggerated sigh of relief: “finally.” when prompted, he explained that it was obvious that this was the path for me. any of my “confusion” over these past few years was just fear manifesting: intimidation about straying from my industry-oriented friends, dread at the thought of going for what i truly want and not getting it. it was the “finally” of a reader who had figured out whodunnit by Chapter 2,  finally getting to see the detective piece together that the killer was right there all along. 
i don’t know how much of that friend’s conviction is true. the thought is nice to contemplate, to believe every once in a while. certainly when i am budgeting times to chip away at applications and planning professors to ask for letters of recommendation, it is reassuring to buy into the idea of a true calling. a purpose that exists for each person to uncover from their depths, right there all along. the veil lifting is my litmus test, the indication that i have matured enough to look my calling in the eye and pursue it.
it is nice to believe it is true. words like these instill a confidence, perhaps undue, that i need to make it through the worst parts of this Fall. to push through the weight of my blanket and convince other people, not just myself, that grad school could be a tangible next step for me. not like when i asked my academic advisor, a week ago, if i might not be ready, compelling her to adamantly affirm, “yes, you are.” i take these words as part of my morning shrine, as well, and work on being that affirmation myself.

Title: i’m a sneaky little scavenger
Author: Allison E. '27
Article Content:
have you ever wanted to furnish an apartment for as little money as possible? are you a sneaky little scavenger?
hee hee hee ha ha ha
here are some ideas, courtesy of me and my amazing summer roommate grace :D
1.  find furniture on the side of the street
in the words of one of my friends, “welcome to the wonderful wastage of the bay area”! i lived in downtown-ish San Jose this summer and there was SO MUCH FURNITURE ABANDONED ON THE SIDE OF THE ROAD (smth smth college students ig) (seriously i think i found at least 35 pieces of furniture on this one street over 2.5 months, including like 6 couches)
classic ikea malm dresser... almost almost decided to bring this one home
unfortunately my roommate only had a twin futon mattress so we couldn't use this
couches are suspiscious
An arrow pointing right
PreviousAn arrow pointing right
Next
generally i would not recommend taking mattresses and couches due to potential small evil critter issues. however, metal, plastic, and even wood are less nefarious. i ended up acquiring an entire bed frame and a room divider thingy (i was sleeping in the living room so this was helpful)
genuinely never realized how much a bedframe improves quality of life, and idek why
privacy yay :D
An arrow pointing right
PreviousAn arrow pointing right
Next
2.  steal cardboard boxes from costco
so uh i did not realize this but there’s a bunch of random table-things that are useful in an apartment. dining room table, desk, nightstand, dresser, etc. etc. that is many items! i did not want to pay for and later get rid of that many items.
solution: STEAL BOXES FROM COSTCO
cardboard boxes from costco are shockingly sturdy objects, AND they come in extremely convenient shapes. the standard cardboard box (rectangular prism) is suboptimal for table use because it’s one convex solid and you can’t put your legs “underneath” the table surface, so instead you must place the box at arms length and eat dinner bent forward in uncomfortable supplication to the cardboard. Costco boxes, on the other hand, are open in the front and provide a convenient place to put your feet and/or other miscellaneous objects! This means they work not only as dinner tables, but as double-tiered nightstands, dresser drawers, and assorted elevated surfaces.
there’s even a little slot at the top where you can put your charger so it doesn’t end up tangled somewhere
 
3.  get yourself a roommate who has family in the area
chairs are kinda hard to acquire without the possibility of also acquiring small evil critter issues, so we borrowed 2 folding lawn chairs from my roommate’s family
these chairs were actually amazingly comfy
4.  make your roommate acquire free stuff from santa clara students
free microwave! and free desk fan thingy! lowkey have not encountered a microwave with a physical windup timer instead of a digit pad, but it was in perfect condition.
highkey SUPER clean, great find by my roommate
5.  what is a trash can? who needs that
all you need are trash bags and a hook (you don’t even need a hook)
[i don’t have a picture but just imagine a large black trash bag hooked to the side of the fridge]
6.  buy a couple things ig
i shelled out for a nice futon mattress to sleep on, a $10 ikea clothesrack, and an $8 rug for shoes. also like $8 for two very sturdy very plastic home depot buckets that turned into footstools, secondary tables, and waterproof surfaces (since all the rest of our surfaces were cardboard )
afterword:
the final product! our living room / my bedroom :D
i have tragically become the stereotype of a true tech bro BUT i did save a lot of money on furniture so i consider that a win. moral of the story? maybe find summer housing that’s already furnished. but also rent is cheaper if you don’t

Title: this pan is going places
Author: Emily P. '28
Article Content:
Two months abroad. One suitcase. And a girl whose favorite MIT alum is none other than American chef and food journalist J. Kenji López-Alt. The result? 4.61 pounds of questionably seasoned cast iron flying a total of 32 hours⁠01a pit stop was made for an older brother’s graduation & a long overdue visit with the grandparents, thus the cumulative 32 hoursto arrive at its final destination: Bordeaux, France. Coincidentally, it’s also where I, Emily Pan, am doing a MISTI!
When I began packing my suitcase about 5 hours before my flight, I had reached a semi-fugue state thanks to dorm-moving exhaustion and poor time management choices. I daydreamed of living a nomadic lifestyle in the distant future, owning nothing but the bare necessities so that I wouldn’t have to relive the detestable and harrowing event that is moving out (and also moving in). In the spirit of such, I decided to pack the things that I deemed essential to my lived experience, things that I would truly need everyday—which happens to include a 10” Lodge skillet and a Babish chef’s knife.
Some context. I am a part of Mince,⁠02Massachusetts Institute of Culinary Experiences, otherwise known as MIT’s fine dining club (except it’s so much more than that!)I live in a cook-for-yourself dorm,⁠03Burton-Conner an estimated 2/3rds of my doomscrolling content is food-related, and I am a proud owner of a small but growing cooking equipment collection, of which the aforementioned pan and knife are a part of. But besides being the most used items in my kitchen, my pan and knife also represent a philosophy that I’ve been trying to exercise: buy it for life.⁠04oh hey, the Lodge cast iron is the first product listed on the buy it for life website! And on NYT Wirecutter!
It goes without saying that part of the practice is the purchase itself: you should buy quality items that can last a lifetime (or more) rather than quantities of disposable or easily damaged items. But I’d argue that it’s perhaps more important to use and maintain these purchases. 
The first seems like a given; except, more often than not, people tend not to use their nicer, more expensive items in an attempt to preserve them, which, for a lot of these things, completely defeats the purpose. And the truth is, so many of these ‘buy it for life’ products only get better with use: leather goods, instruments, quality denim, and of course, the humble cast iron. Use your nice things, everyone!!
The latter varies from item to item, but generally, if we want things to last for a long time, we need to maintain them. For my knife, this just means wiping it down after washing (to avoid rust) and the very occasional visit (like, only one time so far) to the Forge for a poorly executed whetstone sharpening. For my cast iron, it’s a bit of a different story.
I had watched about a dozen Youtube videos and read through 3 or 4 Reddit threads about cast iron maintenance before making my purchase this January. Here she was fresh out the box.
The humble Lodge 10-inch chef collection pre-seasoned skillet, basking in all her glory and beauty.
And here she was a week later…
This image haunts me. A crime scene.
I don’t blame any of my suitemates for this because I totally should have warned them about the one universally agreed upon no-no for cast irons: no soaking in the sink. It’s made of iron, it’s going to rust. Thus began the treacherous journey that is re-seasoning.
Crash course on cast irons: when you get a really thin layer of oil really hot, the fat molecules will start polymerizing to itself and to the pan. Multiple layers of the polymerized fat is what’s known as seasoning, and also what makes cast irons almost non-stick. That’s the basic science, also generally agreed upon. The details of how best to build and maintain a seasoning, however, is a rat’s nest of conflicting information that I don’t plan on going into. 
What I can say is, re-seasoning and maintaining my cast iron has felt a tiny bit like parenthood. It’s tedious, mechanically repetitive. Sometimes it feels like one step forward and then two steps back. There are nights where I’m exhausted and want to leave my pan in the sink for the next morning but nooooooo I have to wash it and dry it and oil it. Yet, watching it grow more and more non-stick has been so rewarding. I told my brother the day I was able to cook scrambled eggs without making a huge mess that I felt like I just watched my kid walk across the stage at graduation.
Flash forward to now, July 2026.⁠05now is actually September 2026... My cast iron is 7,005 kilometers⁠064,353 milesfrom its birthplace of South Pittsburg, Tennessee. Alongside me, she’s been introduced to novel ingredients and recipes, some of French origins and others not. And also like me, though she sometimes has to work overtime, she also gets days off, like when there was that really bad heatwave and since the French don’t believe in air conditioning, experiments had to be put on pause and my diet consisted primarily of cold, refreshing salads. But anyways, I have cooked a variety of things in my cast iron, and I wanted to share some of them!
smash burger
I ate cheese burgers for my first three days in France. It was awesome.
ingredients
lettuce
¼ onion
tomato
 american cheese⁠07so, this is not american cheese & I forgot what it was but it was good
bread of choice
80/20 ground beef 
instructions
Slice tomatoes, set on a paper / kitchen towel, and salt lightly.
Slice onion thin, the thinner the better. 
Preheat pan on medium. Meanwhile, form balls of ground meat with hands. My 10-inch pan fits two patties at a time. Add oil / butter, wait for it to glimmer / sizzle, place patties, and smash! I used the bottom of a pot wrapped with foil.
In the space around the patties, add the onion. Salt everything.
Move onions around as needed, and when the onions reach desired jamminess, remove from pan. 
Simultaneously, keep an eye on the patties. Depending on how well you smashed them, they will take less or more time. Proper smash patties are really only cooked on one side for optimal crust. When it feels like they’ve got a crust, flip, add cheese, and cook only until the cheese starts to melt. Remove from pan.
Toast bread in leftover beef grease.
Assemble and enjoy!
chorizo pesto pasta
The French enjoy a variety of cured meats, which includes the semi-spicy chorizo I used here. In a stroke of pure brilliance,⁠08in other words, I had nothing else in the pantryI added pesto to make this delicious pasta.
ingredients
any store bought pasta
OR
one egg
eyeballed / vibes-based ½ cup of flour
chorizo
pesto
(optional) a little butter
instructions
(optional) Make fresh pasta.
Bring water to boil. If using dried pasta, add pasta now. Also preheat a pan to medium low.
While water is heating up, chop chorizo into roughly ½ inch cubes. Add chorizo cubes to pan.
Chorizo fat will render. Stir occasionally to prevent burning. As the fat renders, the chorizo will get crispy but also tougher, so cook until desired doneness.
Add fresh pasta to boiling water when the chorizo is almost done.
Add cooked pasta to the chorizo pan, as well as a dollop of pesto. 
Stir pasta, chorizo, and pesto passive aggressively. Add pasta water as needed, until pesto and chorizo fat emulsifies.
Taste for salt and adjust with pasta water or pesto as needed
Cut heat, finish with a dab of (optional) butter, stir once more.
Plate and enjoy!
pinkslaw & chickpeas
I owe everything to the Internet Shaquille, my goat.⁠09why chickpeas, but also how chickpeas
ingredients
can of chickpeas (200g)
quarter head of red cabbage
1 medium carrot or 2 small carrots
½ red onion
4 radishes I think
fresh green herbs of choice (I used dill and carrot leaves)
grateable cheese of choice (I used comté)
lime / lemon
olive oil
honey / sugar
instructions
Make slaw ahead of time by adding thinly sliced not-yet-pink vegetables to a container alongside the juice of an entire lime / lemon, a big pinch o’ salt, and a smaller pinch of sugar / squeeze of honey. Toss together and let sit in the fridge for at least an hour.
When ready to eat, rinse and drain chickpeas, add to a flat microwaveable plate, and microwave for ~5 minutes.
Meanwhile, preheat pan. Add a healthy dose of olive oil, and toss in freshly microwaved chickpeas. Add a pinch o’ salt and fry until golden or at desired crispiness. 
(optional) After cutting the heat, I also like to toss the chickpeas with some bouillon powder.
On the side, roughly chop herbs. 
Add ½ of now-indeed-pink slaw, chickpeas, and herbs to the bowl. Taste for salt / acidity levels, grate cheese on top.
Toss and enjoy!

Title: Welcome to our new bloggers!
Author: Chris Peterson SM '13
Article Content:
After much deliberating over the ~100 blogger applications we received this summer, we are happy to introduce you to our new baby bloggers.
We hired 8 baby bloggers —  four first years, and four older-than-first-years —  because that is the number of ‘2027s we expect to see graduating (between senior year and MEngs), and we aim to have rough conservation and continuity of posters.
Their cartoon faces (drawn by our peerless kitty with a pencil Sam Xu on the comms team) are below.
The newest apprentices to the posting guild.
 
In order of top row to bottom, left to right:
Lauren W. ’29, a member of the varsity soccer team (and protege of former jockblogger Emiko P. ’25), may be blogging about the beaches of SoCal, the Ring Premiere, and her ongoing attempts to choose a major, among other things, all while sipping a matcha
Nick R. ’29 believes that one of the lessons of MIT is you don’t pull the ladder up after you, and so whether he’s writing about his fraternity, club hockey, juggling, art, classes, or more, he wants to share his highlights and frustrations, ambitions and regrets, and the parts of himself that he’s learning to reconcile
Emily P. ’28 identifies as an altoids tin of thoughts, hoping to further process experiences into insights through conversations with friends and writing (and art-ing) for an audience, and drawing together a heterogenous community that collectively represents MIT
Leya E. ’30 describes herself as having an unhealthy obsession with hit Sanrio character Cinnamoroll, physics, and indie rock music; we will let readers be the judge of degree, as she blogs her way through the twisty, turny thicket of life decisions
Leanne F. ’30, a recovering artist, would like you to know that if you think you met her on campus, no you didn’t. She has survived haunted monkey bamboo forests and pooping planarians and lived to tell the tale, whether around a homemade sashimi platter in Simmons or here on the internet
Alejandro B. ’30 has only been here a few weeks but already made ample use of Bluebikes for H-Mart runs, enjoyed the view and the people of MacGregor’s B-Entry on the 12th floor, and looks forward to exploring many clubs and classes and telling you about them
Suzuko O. ’30 is interested in asking you invasive questions and potentially answering them himself. We have both eaten horse meat in Kazakhstan (at different times). We keep hiring Tetazoo bloggers without knowing it for some reason and I need to consult the oracles to figure out why.
Joy X. ’29 has already worn Ellie’s face like a mask on the blogs here, here, and here. She often juggles and rides a unicycle to class, and while she used to think she might drop out to join the circus, at the Institute of Hacks, Pranks, and Tomfoolery, she realized she is already there…
Please join me in welcoming the baby bloggers! You’ll see their words (and cartoon faces) joining the blogs in the coming days.

Title: Return to Campus
Author: Victor D. '27
Article Content:
I don’t know how to feel. “How do you feel about your last FDOC⁠01First Day of Classes ?” Great question. It (graduation) doesn’t feel so imminent unless I psyche myself to believe so. I can barely surmise what my life will look or feel like in a month, so how am I supposed to locate this day in my life relative to an event in June? It’s too far. I think thinking about it worries me more than it excites me though. So I’ve chosen for it to be remote, distant, but every “I’m a 4th year senior” incants the inevitable end.
I can scarcely recall my life before college now that I think about it. I remember it conceptually—names, events, classes, places—but seldom does it evoke real emotion in the way that my recent memories do.
So I can lean on my experience graduating high school only to fall through it, a phantasmagorical mist without physicality, only image, an image that feels to belong to me as much as a story I watch on television—which is to say, it no longer belongs to me, it belongs to an otherperson me who I’m not quite sure when I broke from them, lost them, when they died.
So I’m trying to imagine the image of my impending graduation and really I can’t comprehend it. I recently read They Both Die at the End; I wonder about the major theme, carpe diem to the utmost everyday; no kicking the can down the road indefinitely until it’s too late; when death wielding scythe already claws at the door.
So then I think about seizing my days to the fullest and I encounter a library stretching beyond the clouds and into the depths of the Earth, a bookcase of what to me are essentially innumerable combinatorial books upon bookshelves and on an infinitesimal minority I may glean only their title spines, and in their pages when I leaf through another book coalesces in its place while my eyes adrift, and the library itself grows the more I pull from its shelves and read and pull and read…
More done, and less is the proportion complete. If I were to live as though I were to die at the end of each day, I’d be frozen in place as Matteo in They Both Die at the End, unable to leave his room, terrified by risk and choice and combinations thereof.
It’s really a gift to have an inexhaustible library to discover… but alas I won’t be able to do everything, as the more I do the more it feels as though I haven’t done anything. Anyways, rather than fixity in fear, I’m just doing what I want to do now without too much concern of that-which-I-want-to-do-but-don’t-have-time-to-do-now.
Although I can’t do everything, anything is something. So everyday I do progress and exercise something I like: reading, writing, music, studying, walking, playing soccer… none are commensurable, and so I’ll do what I enjoy—shun the Opportunity Cost Demon!

Title: I didn’t know a lot coming into MIT
Author: Jessica Z. '27
Article Content:
One of the most embarrassing memories I have happened during a summer program in high school. We had an introductory class teaching us how to use LaTeX, a typesetting system that can be used to write scientific documents. I, however, did not know what the class was actually about and showed up with a notebook, pencil, and no laptop.
I veryyyyy quickly realized my mistake when everyone pulled out their laptop and started typing, but I was too embarrassed to say anything, so I just sat at my desk and pretended to look busy.⁠01which, as you can imagine, was not very convincing considering I didn't have my laptop lol About ten minutes into the class, the TA walked over to me and jokingly said that since I clearly already knew how to use LaTeX, I could help some of the people around me.
So, instead of spending a few minutes embarrassed to admit to my TA that I didn’t know what LaTeX was so I didn’t bring my laptop, I spent an entire class period embarrassed that the TA probably thought I thought I was too smart to participate. While I wince a lot thinking about this encounter from over four years ago, it’s a pretty good representation of how I’ve historically dealt with embarrassment. I hate looking like I don’t know what I’m doing, even if it’s true, and I hate asking a question that I think I should know the answer to. I also hate the possibility that someone might think I’m incompetent, even if nothing they’ve done suggests that they believe that.
In general, I think embarrassment clouds a lot of my experiences. In high school, I honestly used to get most of my work done by scheduling check-ins with people because I knew I would be too embarrassed to show up empty-handed. It was definitely not sustainable, but for a while, it worked.
All that to say, I cannot think of a period of my life when I was more consistently embarrassed than my first two years of college. In the spirit of being vulnerable, here’s a few things I did my freshman year:
Emailed my first-year advisor to ask why I was double-booked for a class because I didn’t know that recitation was different from lectures
Dropped 6.100A⁠02Introduction to Computer Science Programming because I got a 3% on my first microquiz
Cried in front of my 5.111⁠03Principles of Chemical Science TA after recitation because I failed my first exam, while the next recitation section filed into the classroom
Cried HAPPY tears over getting a C on my 5.12⁠04Organic Chemistry I final because that meant I didn’t have to retake it⁠05thank you PNR
I also didn’t magically figure everything out my sophomore year:
Started and finished more PSETs that I’d like to admit the day they were due
Pulled a few too many all-nighters for Ring Committee⁠06sometimes with other committee members lol
Talked to my advisor about taking a semester off and teared up about three times during our meeting
Andddd even into my junior year, I felt like I was still finding ways to embarrass myself:
Butchered my first industry interview because I misread their job description. I thought their work focused on lead (as in, the material) not lead discovery (aka figuring out what drugs are leading contenders for further studies)
During a final-round interview, a company VP asked how I had heard about them and why I was interested in the company, which was probably my cue to say something thoughtful about their work. Instead, I blanked and told him I had seen their logo on a lot of backpacks while I was living in D.C.⁠07A+ for honesty?
I spent a lot of my first two years at MIT nervous. I was constantly worried about what or how other people seemed to be doing. I also spent a lot of time believing I was making wayyy more “mistakes” than everyone else around me. At some point, I kind of forgot the whole reason I was here was to learn. And learning can feel, unfortunately, kind of embarrassing at times.
If someone had told freshman-year me, “You’re here to learn! Don’t worry!” I probably would have felt an urge to scream at them. Obviously I was taking classes to learn. Now, though, on the brink of my senior year, I realize I didn’t quite understand how much learning required me to become comfortable with other people watching me not know things.
Before college, I never would have reached out to friends for academic help as readily or as casually⁠08many days in Stud5 with boba and PSETs as I do now. I wouldn’t have swallowed my pride enough to repeatedly ask for help when I was three lectures behind or not even sure where to start on a PSET. I wouldn’t have been forced to decide what I actually wanted to devote my time to after realizing I couldn’t take every class or join every club I wanted to. There was absolutely no universe in which high-school me could have dropped a class and felt okay afterwards. I’m also infinitely more comfortable now telling my friends when I’m struggling or frustrated or sad. I’ve gotten better at not ruminating over every tiny “mistake” because I realized there’s no point in being embarrassed about trying to learn something new.
Sometimes I think about how my parents had to grow up so quickly, particularly immigrating to a new country and worrying about finances much more than I have ever had to. I’ve been given this four year period where I can, and I’m expected to, mess up in varying amounts of severity. My parents didn’t have four years carved out for learning more about themselves and the world around them, and they certainly didn’t have time to be embarrassed every time they didn’t know how to do something. I feel so lucky to be in a place where I’m meant to learn, even when every mistake or decision can feel impossibly heavy. 
The exams I failed felt catastrophic but don’t take up any of my mental space today. The awkward interviews and dropped classes are now stories and inside jokes with my friends. The reality is that everyone struggles with learning something here at MIT, even if it doesn’t feel that way. There will always be another thing I don’t know how to do, and I think I’ve finally become a little more okay with that.
To the frosh: you never really stop learning about yourself here, which means you might find yourself embarrassed more than once, and that’s okay! Ask the stupid question, go to office hours for what feels like the tenth time to ask the same question, drop the class if you need to, and tell your friends when you’re struggling. Most importantly, bring your laptop to any LaTeX workshops. And if you don’t, remember that it’s not the end of the world. 
You don’t have to, and certainly don’t, know everything coming into MIT, and I really think that’s how you grow the most <3

Title: how to get from east campus to the student center
Author: Boheng C. '28
Article Content:
you don’t have to care
you don’t have to listen
you don’t have to read
you just have to notice
                                    — maya kaul, ‘19
you already know the fastest path, but you might not know all of them. and there’s so many cool things that you get to see if you don’t take the fastest one.
start by walking out the entrance to the dorm. 
enter building 66 through the doors on the east.
go down the stairwell into the basement.
walk forwards and down the ramp, down down down, and count the poppies lined along the wall, growing short medium tall
stop at the end of the hallway.
look to your right: a double door leading to a ramp, but the right door is propped open and doesn’t seem to be able to close. there’s a pipe jutting out of the ceiling which stops it from swinging shut. how odd.
look to your center: another double door, this time sealed shut with one lock and one handle.
look to your left.
there’s something there, isn’t there?
there’s something there which might help you enter new locations. look for it. look for it, on the ground, next to the elevators, in the long hallway; comb through the ceiling lights and doorframes and the vending machine. 
did you find it?
go back the way you came, back up the ramp, and continue past the stairwell.
go forward until the end of the hallway.
make a right turn.
walk until you find a water fountain and drink from it, perceive the bitter cold sharp water as it ebbs into your mouth, and notice the fountain of youth to your left, dried up and exhausted of its former life.
continue down the basement hallway until the first junction, and turn right there.
turn left again.
take a paper cup (you brought a paper cup, right?) and fill it up with hot chocolate at the vending machine, two dollars, and ponder your hot chocolate with foam in this unremembered corner of the stata center, five meters beneath the grandeur of an auditorium lecture hall, condemned to oblivion, for just two dollars.
was this place forgotten on purpose or by accident?
walk further along the corridor until you reach the door to a stairwell. enter it.
watch the outlines of dirt footprints on the walls as they meander towards the top.
go back out and go through the garage door nearby.
turn left then right into the loading docks without descending into the parking lot.
choose — choose between keyboards and desks and chairs and refrigerators with dark growths and cracked monitors leaking their blood of liquid crystal.
go down the stairs at the end. 
walk straight until you get to the car lane entering the parking lot.
turn right and left on the sidewalk until the door, then walk through until you get to an odd vending machine and read the sign:
go back, back through the loading docks silent basement vending machines fountain of youth, back and back until the south stairwell of building 26, and take it up to the first floor and smell the drunken scent of overripe bananas, imbibe the air, and realize that there’s a kettle and packets of hot chocolate in front of you, and that you didn’t have to pay two dollars at the basement vending machine earlier.
head into building 16 and up the short stairs to building 8.
just before reaching the infinite corridor, look up at the ceiling, past the network of dangling pipes. 
it reads GULLIBLE.
go forwards a bit and turn right, into the stairs down into the basement.
make a right and soon after a left until you get to what looks like an elevator.
is it an elevator?
walk back into the long corridor going west.
stop at the shelves full of old printers and books and manila folders and screws and cryptic circuit boards and pamphlets and water bottles.
turn right and walk until you reach building 13.
find a short door to the right of two vent openings. 
notice that the bottom vent has three of its four screws missing, while the top vent is intact.
continue forwards and turn left.
look up at the pipes suspended from the ceiling, contorting and wrapping and dancing around themselves.
go forwards through the hallway, notice behind you the surveillance camera mounted at eye level, bulbous shadowy lens watching through the cover.
go to the end of the hallway in building 9, before it makes a bend.

run straight across massachusetts ave. because it’s already late, the street and its cars long asleep, the world powerless to stop you.

This generally means that you have to take 4 PE classes (though of course you are welcome to more if you wish) throughout your time at MIT, and you also have to know how to swim. Title: All the 2026 i3 videos megapost
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content:
MIT likes to be unique in many ways: majors are called courses, everything from classes to buildings are numbered, and maybe more unexpectedly, MIT has a very unique dorm set-up. Dorms are not filtered by class year, there are no special “honors” dorms, and no dorm is meant to be “nicer” or an “upgrade” to others.⁠01Though, admittedly, some dorms are nicer due to having more recent renovations/opening dates.
The biggest distinguishing factor between MIT dorms is each’s tight-knit and well-defined community. Undergrads take part in multiple campus-wide dorm exploratory events⁠02Campus Preview Weekend in April for accepted students, and Residence Exploration the week before classes start in the fall for freshmen. to understand each dorm’s culture and where they want to live.
In order to help with this decision process, dorms make/compile Interactive Introduction to the Institute (I3) videos for students to explore the dorms and their culture each year. These are posted under each dorm on MIT’s Housing and Residential Services website. 
The following, in alphabetical order by dorm, are all the of 2026 i3 videos embedded for easier access. Take a look!
Note that New House has its 6 floors submit their own i3 videos, all of which you can access here separately. Simmons did not submit a 2026 i3 video, but last year’s is available here.

Title: i went to the ig nobels!
Author: Ellie F. '28
Article Content:
It’s funny how optimistic summer makes me. Every August, I sign up for more classes than ever and dream about the clubs I’ll join and the adventures I’ll have over in Cloud Cuckoo Campus, where psets are fun and get done in a reasonable amount of time and I never have to sacrifice anything, ever. It’s falling in love with someone you see once a year–highly unrealistic, I suppose, but can you help it? Isn’t it fun?
All this to say I thought I was some hot stuff going into last fall, and it ended in a nontrivial amount of tears. But before it ended, I’d made up my mind to shoot my shot with the Ig Nobel Prize and either ask, guilt trip, or plead my way into a press pass. This was much easier than I had anticipated.
I went to the ceremony and had a life changing experience, et cetera and so on, and I left with about an hour of footage. I’d make a vlog, and it would be fun, and I’d be done in a month or so, and then maybe I’d make a room tour because my roommate and I finally put up decorations after throwing the idea around for all of freshman year.
The fall semester ended (I didn’t edit). I went home for winter break (I didn’t edit). I came back to campus for all of IAP (did not edit). I had no plans for all of spring break (can you see the pattern yet). So that leaves the summer.
I moved into a two bed one bath house in California and bought groceries and new shoes from the shopping center three pedestrian crossings away. I hung up my shirts in a color gradient and learned which drawers in the kitchen didn’t slide out quite right. And when I was settled in, I was resolved that this time, really, I would edit the vlog.
My summer ended up being the Caltrain on more evenings than not, crowding myself in with the Giants fans in orange and young urban professionals leaving the office but still working on the way home. I’ll tell you about it more another day. But my summer certainly wasn’t Adobe Premiere.
My new mantra was to do it when I got home, to Arkansas. That’s where my excuses ran out. I’d sit down at my computer each evening, meaning to watch through my interviews and write a script. I had nothing else to do, after all. Instead, I ended up at the piano, relearning old songs and the feeling of the stretch in my hands.
It’s awful that only a hard deadline could make me finish this project. Honestly, I don’t like what that says about me. I’m hoping that it’s not an unchangeable fact, and I’m hoping that this is the semester where I change it, but then I look at my classes and despair just a little.
The fall equinox isn’t for another few weeks, and I’m dreaming again. I can’t help myself, and, well, it’s really, terribly fun.

Title: i did nothing these past two years, part 1
Author: Boheng C. '28
Article Content:
this morning, i got kicked out of my lab.
of course, it felt like a surprise when i heard for the first time. it was a surprise. had it not been just weeks before when i trod headfirst into that office, illuminated by the hot summertime glow of killian court, a bit suffocating in its boisterous proclamations of lemonade encased in sweat and retreat to air-conditioned dorms, and had i not declared bright-eyed to my postdoc supervisor that i wanted to continue this research for another semester? and had he not said yes, yes of course? and in that moment, had i not felt that i was meant to be there? that i belonged? that i, after all, was truly there?
or had those few weeks grown monstrously into months already, and had that hot summertime glow been instead the soft vernal midday sun, and had the buds of spring barely emerged from their snowy blanket?
what have i been doing all these months?
what have i been doing for two years?
 
the research was fun. i loved it even, i loved continuum mechanics and calculus of variations and i loved making all the plots and doing fourier transforms. i loved being able to work on the research wherever i wanted. i loved watching terms cancel out and variables dance around the page. in short, it was everything that i could’ve asked for in a urop⁠01undergraduate research opportunity. of course, it was a bit abstract, and sometimes difficult to see how the assumptions translated into physicality, but i felt like i was doing something.
and yet, i can only ask why i spent so little time on the research. certainly, i was busy and i had less time than i wished that was left over for the urop. but time and time again, when faced with the choice to do something i dearly enjoyed, i said no.
and so, this morning, when i declared bright-eyed to my pi⁠02principal investigator that i wanted to continue this research for another semester: “i think not.”

Title: A Recipe for Staying Whimsical
Author: Richard O. '28
Article Content:
With the “-ber” months right around the corner, it’s very easy to get caught up in things like schoolwork, college applications, exams, projects, and other stressful activities that make it hard for you to make time for yourself. But in order to make sure you don’t burn yourself out, it’s sometimes helpful to set aside an hour or two where you step away from everything and take time to enjoy some of the small things you love, because the most important part of life is experiencing and not staring at a computer screen or assignments for hours on end with no breaks. So today I decided to whip up a recipe for staying whimsical that you can bake on your own anytime you’re hungry for a break.
Ingredients:
1 quart of an optimistic mindset
5 tablespoons of your favorite songs
1 bowl (or two) of your favorite snacks or a pint of ice cream
3 cups of positive affirmations
3 tbsp of your proudest memories or moments
A close app feature on on all social media services and online assignments
1/2 cup of a friend or family member you can talk to
1 version of you that will figure things out
2 mixing bowls
A spatula/whisk
A chopping board
An oven (though a room, library, or sidewalk with ample sunlight is preferred as a substitute)
Plastic wrap
A baking pan
Instructions:
Step 1. Dissociate from expectations:
To get started, take the version of you that will figure things out and separate all expectations for yourself on the chopping board.
Move the excess expectations aside
Place the remaining version of you in a mixing bowl and pour in the quart of an optimistic mindset. 
 
Step 2. Relax:
Allow the bowl containing you and the optimistic mindset to rest for 15 mins. 
In your second mixing bowl, add the following dry ingredients: 
5 tablespoons of your favorite songs
1 bowl or two of your favorite snacks or a cup of ice cream
3 cups of positive affirmations
Mix until satisfied.
Pour the dry ingredients into the bowl containing you and the optimistic mindset
Mix until all the ingredients are blended together
Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and allow to rest and rise for at least 1 hour
 
Step 3. Prep the Oven/Substitutes 
If using an oven, check to make sure your oven is turned off (unless your favorite snack actually requires you to bake something and they’re still baking)
If you didn’t acquire the preferred substitutes to the oven, you now need to acquire them
Preheat the substitutes to a temperature associated with a decent amount of sunlight in the location of your choice
If frequent sunlight is unavailable, a room with windows will suffice
 
Step 4. More Mixing and Baking
Take your mixing bowl of primary ingredients and remove the plastic wrap
Sprinkle in the 3 tbsp of your proudest memories or moments and fold into the mixture
Pour the mixture into a baking pan
Lightly coat the mixture with the close app feature on on all social media services and school assignments
Place the baking pan in the preheated substitute and set another 1 hour timer.
While waiting, you can optionally put the 1/2 cup of a friend or family member you can talk to on a pan on medium heat and let simmer for at least 20 mins to add to the garnish
After 1hr, check to see if the items are ready to be removed
If not check back every 20 minutes until the texture is soft, fluffy, and ready to come out of its oven of choice
 
Step 5. Garnish and Enjoy
Finally, remove the pan from the oven and let cool for 15 minutes
On the chopping board take the leftover expectations from before and cut them into finely sliced goals and toss out any parts of the expectations that would spoil the final product or don’t seem to look appetizing. 
If you used the friend or family member you can talk to in this recipe, add the sliced goals in the same pan and mix them together.
Coat the cooled off version of yourself with the garnish and enjoy!

Title: last week, i failed at a jigsaw puzzle and knot theory
Author: Aiden H. '28
Article Content:
This past week, I made the mistake of trying to have a Sunday morning brunch, no reservation. After driving 20 minutes to the best brunch place around with my mom, sister, and girlfriend, none of us were surprised to learn we would have to wait at minimum another 20 before being sat.
And so began the saga.
To kill the time we rounded the corner to a cutesy puzzle and games store. After messing around with Lego flowers, Calico critters, and petting the live bunny they have randomly hanging around, I stumbled upon this beauty:
Priced at a relatively cheap $25, I thought a 1000 piece puzzle might be a little bit of a stretch considering I was leaving Colorado and heading back to MIT at 5 AM Wednesday morning but bought it anyway. Besides, at the point that you’re doing a puzzle, how much of a difference is 500 versus 1000 pieces? Also it’s a pretty distinctive and bright puzzle, so the pieces should be pretty easy to delineate.
Wrong.
I have a bad history with jigsaw puzzles. I always turn to them in a time of productivity crisis (see: COVID lockdown and summer breaks) when I feel bad if I just rot on my phone all day, but I don’t necessarily want to do actually productive work. A similar feeling is reached by reading excessive amounts or tracking my steps.
So what came upon me to believe that my girlfriend and I could crank out a 1000 piece puzzle in 48 hours? Narcissism and amnesia.
We started the first day strong enough, cranking out the edges in 1.5 New Girl episodes/45 minutes. Then disaster hit. I made the awful suggestion of starting at the bottom because the flowers were more distinctive than the mass of yellow above. A whopping six hours into the puzzle, we had only gotten this far:
The next day was much of the same, spending hours upon hours trying to speed run this god-forsaken puzzle, only to be here upon midnight:
With less than 24 hours left before my flight to Boston, we gave up on the puzzle.
***
My return to campus was as normal as ever. I picked up all of my summer storage boxes and said hi to friends as I made my way down the hall to my room, only to be faced with puzzle number two: untangling my fairy lights.
Like anyone under 30 with questionable taste, I have fairy string lights hung up around my dorm room to offset the harsh Walmart-brand overhead lighting that graces MIT dorms. Amongst the rush of packing and simultaneously half-passing my finals in the spring, my past self decided the best decision at the time was to rip-them-off-the-wall-and-shove-them-into-a-box-as-fast-as-possible, which admittedly did not help present-day Aiden when trying to untangle said lights.
I sat on my floor for genuinely an hour and a half trying both possible forms of detangling (trying to methodologically follow each strand and untangle one by one, and flailing it around until it miraculously untangles), of which neither were successful.
Sitting there angry and sweating, I noticed that my tangle of fairy lights looks a lot like a mathematical knot (and I guess a literal one), which is something I know nothing about but have always been interested in. So after 30 minutes of intense Wikipedia-ing and watching simplified YouTube videos, I learned my first fact about knot theory: unknotting numbers. Apparently the unknotting number is the minimum number of moves⁠01Of which I think only some are valid? Can someone tell me if this definition means the minimum number of the three Reidemeister moves? it takes to turn a knot into an unknot, which is just math-ese for circle.⁠02but circle is also math so what the hell I also learned/AI-overviewed some constraints, learning that the unknotting number of any knots is always less than half the knot’s crossing number.
But wait wait wait, as learning too much would ruin my night and prove me a dumbass once again. Technically in math a knot must be “closed” so that all the end are connected, which is,  in all fair, completely ridiculous. Shoelaces? Not a knot. Rope? Not a knot. Ribbons? Not a knot. A circle? Definitely a knot but again not because it’s an unknot. (side note but Dr. Seuss would love knot theory).
My fairy lights? Not a knot.
Looking at my fairy lights again, I felt equally as stuck and now also bad at math. But knot or not,⁠03see what i did there I became convinced by their complexity to have at least a not-a-(un)knotting number of at least 74.
I sat down, analyzed it from all sides like those Rubiks cube guys, and pulled one string from the middle. I kid you not, in the most this-whole-thing-was-scripted way, the entire thing of lights came undone across my lap and was able to string out perfectly across my floor.
It turns out it had an “unknotting” number of 1. Like always, I made everything too complicated.
But look at that, I solved a puzzle.
***
In a very loose metaphor that is definitely not a stretch, I can’t help but feel like these experiences were premonitions on the coming semester.⁠04I’ve noticed that whenever I have something big/notable/minorly important coming up, I take everything around me as some sort of sign. I have no idea why.
Going into freshman year, I had the normal anxieties about moving to college. Most of these were social; will I have friends, like the dining halls, have enough personal space, etc. etc.? My concerns were solely about being able to survive and thrive in the lived experience of being at MIT. After a less-than-stellar freshman experience, I returned to sophomore year fearing things that I had felt become true: isolation, boredom, and stress at college.
Returning for a third time, though, I find that my nerves have been exacerbated but shifted. For the first time coming back, I feel not overwhelmed by the experinece of going to college, but my going to MIT. I feel unable to perform at a level that makes me feel confident–whether it be getting things done on time or literally being able to understand what is happening around me. I’m terrified of actual failure.
This is a pretty common sentiment at MIT. Call it imposter syndrome or whatever, but actually having a taste for MIT makes me feel less like an imposter and more like someone who just can’t handle it all again. I’m not anxiously dreaming up a difficulty in workload, I know it exists.
This is also not a common sentiment at MIT. Most people come to MIT and have an adjustment period where they learn school can be actually hard, but they get over this feeling as time goes on, and eventually as an upperclassman it just feels like school and not battling a dragon. I feel like I’m Benjamin Button-ing through these emotions. Freshman year academics? Totally fine and I would encourage you not to be stressed. Junior year? I’d shit my pants.
But then again everything is always a happy-ish medium. I will almost definitely be stressed this semester. I will also not experience anything I haven’t survived before. Everything will be manageable, I just need to find a way to manage myself going into it.
I guess only time will tell?

I saw what life could be like post MIT, and I saw all of my SF-based friends settled and growing in a way that I had never quite seen myself. I was a rising college senior, and they were all working adults, many of them my age or younger yet much more weathered in years of experience in the Real World. I felt young, fresh, and naive.
It was hard to leave; it was easy to get sucked into the rush of it all. Everyone was doing such important work that would change the world, that had millions of dollars attached to them and even more. The work I was doing was glamorous or at least attached to glamorous causes, and I’ll be damned if I don’t admit that I loved it because it was so grand, so sexy. San Francisco had causes worth believing in and I’d loved it.
And yet, and yet—
I’m back in Boston now. I’m here on campus in my floor shirt, greeting fresh faces, hugging old friends. I ran my gameshow REX event ⁠04a gameshow with two parts: a spelling bee comedy show (which i riffed off one of my fav comedians), and something else called "dormspam or the onion" which goes into the insane and hilarious things that have happened on the mit undergrad mailing lists... and you guess whether a headline is based off that or the onion. i'll let your brain fill out the rest :P and was met with a lot of enthusiasm in all their ayes and nyes, unsuspecting frosh victims falling into all the right jokes as they spelt the wrong words, and roasts and impressive displays of knowledge that I didn’t even expect. ⁠05genuinely how does someone know what an umlaut is and how to spell Côte d'Ivoire off the bat??? I walked to Next Dining with Conner 2⁠06my amazing floor <3 and Luna and Katelyn got stuck in line at Hibachi as everyone who tries to get Hibachi at Next always do, because it’s just that good. I came back from dinner to take a nap on my Twin XL mattress with a sheet and pillow that I stole from Phoenix, which happened after an hour long yap session where I lounged in his hammock and we gossiped about classes. I hung around the B1ners⁠07what we call people who live on burton one at their destroy-the-wall event to snipe Veronica, but also to cheer on the frosh breaking the wall and to talk about which watermelons are the best watermelons. I feel old, a little tired, and all too familiar with this campus and its cobbled pieces of red brick, marbled columns, and brutalist concrete.
I love to linger. In San Francisco, everyone always has somewhere to be, and the only place that makes sense to linger at is work when you have a deadline to hit. Here in Boston, we’re not in a rush; none of us really have anywhere to be—at least not yet—and we all linger around, chatting about where we’re from, what we do, and the uncertainty of where we are going to next.
It’s good to be back.

Title: Just Released: Report of MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use
Author: Chris Peterson SM '13
Article Content:
In January, MIT launched the Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training.
Today, President Kornbluth announced the final report of the committee. I have been spending my morning reading (and listening) to it, and I think it is one of the most important reports about MIT and its education in many years.
In her announcement, President Kornbluth wrote:
As the report makes clear, MIT was founded to help human beings develop their own powers of discovery, problem solving, and invention. That is still and will always be our essential work.
Against that backdrop, AI presents itself to us as a kind of superpower, with both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks. Our challenge now is to derive its benefits and counteract its harms, as we strive “to define and foster the highest-quality residential education – of humans, by humans, in support of human flourishing, and for the betterment of humankind.”
…But far and away the most important work will be cultural. As a community, we need to arrive at a shared understanding of the proper role of AI in education at MIT and in our life together on campus, along with shared norms and values around what we can properly do with these new tools, and what we should expect from and owe to one another.
MIT has deep ties to the birth and development of AI and – through our researchers and our graduates – to its future evolution. We therefore have a duty to prepare our students to know when and how to use AI effectively, wisely, ethically, and responsibly, and when not to use it at all. And we need to equip them to apply these formative personal lessons in whatever work they choose to do in the world.
…MIT is and must always be a place that activates the human mind and spirit and that unites creative people in fulfilling the Institute’s great mission. As we define the Institute’s next chapter, AI will test our commitment to that educational ideal. For the sake of our students, for the future of MIT and for the shape of our sector and our society, it’s imperative that we get this right.
I encourage anyone interested in MIT and our education to read it —  whether you are a prospective student/parent, an alum, or an teacher here or elsewhere. It shows the best of MIT’s reports: thoughtful, deliberative, and deep, rooted in institutional history while looking forward to the world as we find it.
I haven’t blogged much about AI, not because I don’t have thoughts, but because I haven’t been sure what to say. The technology has been changing rapidly. Many MIT alumni —  people I personally know, in some cases since they were in high school —  are involved on all conceivable sides of the debate and at every level of the sociotechnical stack. I’ve experimented with student AI use —  and student AI prohibition —  in my teaching in CMS/W. We’ve committed to not using generative AI on the blogs, and we have no plans to adopt it⁠01Indeed, under MIT’s current information protection policies, we would not be permitted to do so. in other parts of our admissions reading or selection apparatus. At the same time, I have used LLMs to help me with orphaned coding projects,⁠02Like the longstanding goal of being able to subscribe to the blogs via RSS -> newsletter a la Substack, god willing one day I will defeat you. or to find typos or informational inconsistencies across 20+ years of posts.
In many blog posts over the years, I (and others) have talked about the idea of following compasses over maps in conditions of uncertainty. When you don’t know the destination or the route, you have to steer by fixed points: the principles and philosophies that are important to you as an individual and as an institution.
I am grateful that today President Kornbluth, and this report, articulated some of those fixed points on behalf of MIT: that the Institute exists “of humans, by humans, in support of human flourishing, and for the betterment of humankind.”
In the comments below, I’ll share some of my favorite excerpts from the report as I work through it, and I invite any readers to join me in the exercise. Together, in community, we can make meaning together, pointing towards the star we collectively pursue amidst the gathering clouds.

Title: two homes
Author: Veronica P. '27
Article Content:
Yesterday, I went thrifting.
When I thrift, I am a girl on a mission. With far too many options and far too little gems, I must be swift and decisive, methodically and quickly moving my way down the racks, pushing hanger after hanger, making split second judgment after judgment.
But yesterday, something gave me pause.
It was a polo: pretty standard, visibly not my size, and (to be frank) kinda ugly. But there, on the breast, was the logo of my old catholic preschool- the place I’d learned my months of the year and animal sounds and how to spell my name.
Though amused, I moved on, but once I’d noticed it, I couldn’t quite shake it. In blue- the gym uniform I donned each day in my middle school locker room. In green- the sweat-wicking shirts of the local running club I’d spot on early mornings. In yellow- the high school baseball shirts worn by the team every game day.
Suddenly, I realized how much I’d taken for granted constantly being surrounded by semblances of home, by remnants of memories.
I can do what I can. I can lay out in my hammock and soak in the Houston heat till I’m sunburnt and sticky with sweat. I can drive down my neighborhood streets a million times a day and memorize every yard sign, count the high school parking lot stickers adorned on the cars passing by. I can fill my lungs up to capacity with the smell of my best friend’s house, till there’s no room left for me to laugh or scream or cry. I can stuff myself full of my mom’s chicken, the one she’d made just because she knew it was my favorite, even when she wasn’t planning on cooking at all.
I can see her trying too- staring at me a second too long across the kitchen table, squeezing me a bit tighter than normal, visiting my room more often for no particular reason at all.
It’s how you cope when you know things will never quite be the same; when you know that one can return to these people and these places, but they won’t be those same people or places you’d once known. My experience of MIT will send me back a different person, viewing familiarities with a newfound, unfamiliar perspective. Knowing this, I do my best to be mindful of every nuance and appreciative of every detail in these last months at home.
However, as I drive my car its final miles and read my last few books in that backyard hammock, I find myself seized by a sense of restlessness. I’m impatient to reach this next period in my life, that will be stressful and unfamiliar and busy and eventful. And the more I look around my home, the more I think “I love you, but wow, am I ready to leave you.” The muscles of my soul, longing for the opportunity to feel and fear and push, know they would otherwise atrophy. It’s remarkable, really, how these things come around right when you need them; that you can leave those objects of your heart before you grow resentful towards them, so that they can remain as such.
And, who knows. Maybe, in a few year’s time, I’ll flip through the racks of the thrift stores of Boston. I’ll see a shirt that reminds me of a memory far gone, pause, and smile.
What a joy it is to get to have two homes.
